strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful theoretical issue: prior diffusiveness should contribute an additive burn-in cost rather than multiply the long-horizon minimax rate. The resulting asymptotic Gaussian-bandit bound is potentially useful and sharper than the cited prior analyses.

The generalized elliptical-potential lemma is an original and broadly relevant technical contribution. Allowing arbitrary positive-definite initialization and exponents p in [0,1] directly addresses the regime needed by the regret proof.

The posterior-sampling regret decomposition and application of the new potential lemma are conceptually clean. Most of the main Gaussian argument appears repairable without changing its asymptotic conclusion.
The lower bound usefully demonstrates a burn-in cost of the claimed order for important prior families, including isotropic and polynomial-spectrum covariances.

The manuscript is generally well organized, clearly motivates its contribution, and candidly discusses limitations concerning Bayesian regret, prior specification, and log-concavity. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: The exact proof of Theorem 1 contains a Gaussian concentration error. Conditional on the history, (1/2)||hat(theta)_t-theta_*||^2_{V_t} is chi-squared with d degrees of freedom, so the chosen beta must satisfy beta^2=2(d+s), not d+s. Consequently the asserted failure probability and the theorem's displayed constants do not follow as written. The asymptotic corollary is likely recoverable by changing constants, but the stated theorem is unsupported.

The strongly log-concave extension is false under its stated assumptions because the noise is not required to have mean zero. The regret definition includes the realized reward, so nonzero-mean strongly log-concave noise contributes a linear-in-T term and invalidates the posterior-sampling identity used in the proof. A zero-mean assumption or a pseudo-regret definition is necessary.

The proof of Theorem 9 also writes the likelihood as log p_W(A_s^T theta), omitting the observed residual R_{s+1}-A_s^T theta, and invokes the second-moment bound from the Gaussian proof without establishing the required covariance domination for strongly log-concave posteriors. These omissions make this advertised generalization insufficiently justified.

The proof of Lemma 14 ends abruptly after setting the chaining parameters and never derives the claimed norm-concentration inequality. It also inconsistently defines the process using Sigma^{-1/2} and later Sigma^{1/2}. This materially weakens reproducibility of the non-Gaussian result.

The lower-bound appendix has several indexing and scope inconsistencies: Lemma 12's displayed eigenvalue sum does not match the Weyl calculation; the final summation uses t=0,...,T despite a T-round regret definition; and Lemma 10 assumes actions have norm exactly r although Theorem 6 permits the entire ball and claims to cover arbitrary policies. The main lower-bound statement may be recoverable, but the current proof needs careful revision.

There are additional presentation errors in technical statements, including V_{T+1}/V_1 instead of V_T/V_0 at the end of the elliptical-potential proof and a boundary-case problem in Corollary 7 for min(T,d)=1. Taken together with the incomplete appendix, these prevent readers from reliably using the exact results without reconstructing proofs themselves.

The paper is theoretically promising, but multiple theorem-level gaps—especially the false-as-stated non-Gaussian extension—require revision before acceptance. The honest limitations section does not acknowledge these mathematical restrictions.

strengths: The main Gaussian result is significant if correct: Theorem 1 separates the prior-dependent burn-in term from the long-run minimax term, yielding an essentially O~(σd√T + dr√Tr(Σ0)) Bayesian-regret bound instead of multiplicative dependence on prior diffusiveness.

The generalized elliptical-potential lemma is an original and potentially reusable technical contribution. It handles arbitrary positive-definite initialization and fractional exponents, and the manuscript provides a substantial proof rather than treating it as a black box.

The paper is largely self-contained and clearly organized for a theoretical submission. It states explicit constants, supplies proofs in the supplement, relates the upper bound to lower bounds, and honestly identifies limitations involving Bayesian regret, prior misspecification, and log-concavity.
No experiments or code are necessary for the principal mathematical contribution, and there are no apparent research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The proof of the strongly log-concave extension is not sound as written. Lemma 14 claims concentration of ||X||_{Σ^{-1}} for any Σ-sub-Gaussian X, although sub-Gaussianity is defined after centering and places no restriction on E[X]; a deterministic vector with arbitrarily large mean is an immediate counterexample. The application also jumps from concentration of one posterior draw to concentration of the difference of two posterior draws without establishing the required conditional sub-Gaussian parameter. This leaves Theorem 9 unsupported, even if a centered-difference argument may repair it.

The non-Gaussian posterior formula in Appendix B.1 is incorrect: the likelihood should contain p_W(R_{s+1}−A_s^Tθ), not p_W(A_s^Tθ). Moreover, P_W is not required to have zero mean, despite regret being defined using the realized reward. These omissions make the stated model and theorem formally inconsistent.

The lower-bound proof contains a concrete indexing error. Lemma 12 states a sum from i=t+1, but projecting out u_{t,1} and accounting for a rank-t update leaves eigenvalues beginning at i=t+2. The displayed transition from the Weyl bound to an infimum over a (t+1)-dimensional subspace has the same off-by-one mistake. The final weaker Theorem 6 may be recoverable by retaining additional tail terms, but that repair is absent.

Lemma 10 treats every selected action as having norm exactly r, whereas Theorem 6 permits actions in the closed ball ||a||≤r and claims the result for every policy. A reduction to boundary actions or an argument based on conditional expected reward is needed.

Presentation and reproducibility are weakened by numerous consequential slips rather than merely cosmetic typos: inconsistent time ranges in the lower-bound summation, a switch between Σ^{-1/2}X and Σ^{1/2}X in the proof of Lemma 14, unstated positive-definiteness needed for Σ0^{-1}, and omitted justification for posterior covariance bounds in the non-Gaussian case. These make it difficult to verify all advertised results reliably.

The work has meaningful originality and likely contains a valid core Gaussian upper bound, but two advertised contributions—the lower-bound proof and especially the general strongly log-concave theorem—require nontrivial correction. For a proof-driven paper, these unresolved soundness issues outweigh the contribution in its current form.

strengths: Soundness: The central Gaussian result is supported by a detailed, largely convincing proof. The posterior-sampling regret identity, concentration argument, and application of the new potential lemma yield the claimed additive bound of roughly σd√T + dr√Tr(Σ₀), rather than multiplying the long-run term by prior diffusiveness.

Originality: Lemma 3 is a useful generalization of the elliptical-potential lemma. Allowing arbitrary positive-definite initialization and exponents p∈[0,1], with an explicit trace-based burn-in term, appears technically novel and potentially useful beyond this particular analysis.

Significance: Separating prior-dependent burn-in from asymptotic noise-dependent regret gives a clearer account of how diffuse priors affect Thompson sampling. The isotropic and polynomial-spectrum lower-bound specializations show that the burn-in dependence can be unavoidable in important regimes.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is concise, well organized, and mostly self-contained, with explicit constants, assumptions, and appendix proofs. As a theoretical paper it does not require datasets or experimental code to reproduce its main claims.
The limitations section appropriately identifies dependence on log-concavity, Bayesian regret, and a well-specified prior. I found no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The strongly-log-concave extension, Theorem 9, is not correct as stated unless the noise is additionally assumed to have mean zero or regret is redefined as pseudo-regret. The paper defines regret using the realized reward R and drops the noise expectation in its decomposition. Translating any strongly log-concave noise distribution preserves its curvature but can add an arbitrarily large linear-in-T regret term.

The proof of the lower bound has a gap as written: Lemma 10 asserts ‖A_t‖=r even though Theorem 6 allows actions in the full ball ‖A_t‖≤r and quantifies over arbitrary policies. A related inequality using A_t/r may repair this, but the manuscript does not provide it. The appendix also contains inconsistent round/index ranges, including summation through t=T for a T-round regret and an apparent off-by-one in Lemma 12.

Several errors reduce proof checkability in the log-concave section. The posterior likelihood is written as p_W(A_sᵀθ), omitting the observed residual R_{s+1}−A_sᵀθ, and the proof of Lemma 14 switches inconsistently between Σ^{-1/2}X and Σ^{1/2}X. The intended curvature and whitening arguments are recoverable, but the current statements should be corrected.

The lower bound matches the advertised burn-in term only for selected spectral families and principally when T≥d; it is not an instance-wise match for arbitrary Σ₀. Consequently, claims such as near-optimality in “most parameter regimes” are stronger than what the presented lower bounds directly establish.

Overall, the main Gaussian upper-bound contribution appears sound and meaningful, but the false-as-stated extension and lower-bound proof gap warrant revision, placing the paper at weak accept rather than a clear accept.
